extracted.intended_audience: writers, orators, and students of rhetoric and literary style (especially those seeking the 'sublime')
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for achieving sublimity in prose and poetry: principles of grandeur, arrangement, diction, rhythm, and the use of figures (metaphor, hyperbole, simile) that elevate writing beyond mere correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur over faultless neatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater excellences, though not everywhere equally sustained, ought always to be voted to the first place in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer loftiness and 'grandeur of soul' even if an author makes occasional oversights; a faultless style (always neat and pretty) is inferior to occasional majestic greatness. Examples: Homer and Pindar (unequal but sublime) vs Apollonius and Bacchylides (consistently neat but lesser in value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loftiness outweighs number of merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Loftiness (sublimity) is a higher standard than the mere number or variety of merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author with many second-best qualities (like Hyperides) may be versatile but still not sublime; a single supreme mastery (Demosthenes' impassioned eloquence) can surpass many lesser excellences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong feeling, energy, and the power to rouse emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity requires strong feeling, energy, and the ability to kindle terror or powerful emotion in readers/hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An orator/writer who 'exhibits strong feeling' and 'sends out flash after flash' attains sublimity; mere polish and wit without passion (Hyperides' wit vs Demosthenes' passion) will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: One masterly stroke can redeem errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A single grand and masterly stroke can redeem an author's many errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting all the blunders of great masters would still leave a vastly larger proportion of perfect passages; posterity crowns those who achieve absolute perfection in parts despite faults elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use art as an ally to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine natural genius with art/technique to achieve perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since avoidance of error is usually the gift of art and high though unequal excellence is the attribute of genius, it is proper to call in art as an ally to nature; the combined resources can produce the best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole must be drawn with restraint and arise naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Know where to draw the line in hyperbole; if overstepped the effect is spoilt by overstraining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective hyperbole is often 'in disguise' and grows naturally out of the circumstances (e.g., Thucydides' and Herodotus' accounts); extravagant, forced hyperbole (Isocrates' flourish) appears childish and warns the audience not to believe the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole may increase or lessen argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration can be used either to magnify or to diminish (extenuate) — it is common to both uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperboles may make an opponent's argument seem smaller or heighten a subject; comedic extravagances gain credence by humour where passions lie in pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement/harmony of words elevates the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere arrangement of words (composition, harmony, modulation) is a principal source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition is akin to musical harmony; rhythm, mutual relation of words, and the 'rounding of the period' can win, delight, exalt the soul, and dispose the hearer to sympathize with the speaker's feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulation, metre, and placement of words matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Modulation (cadence/measure) and the placement or length of syllables affect how grandeur strikes the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Demosthenes' decree moving in dactylic heroic measure; reserving certain words to the end produces weight. Altering or abridging syllables can 'cripple' grandeur or dissipate abrupt force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity arises from the organic unity of particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause may derive sublimity from the joint contributions of a number of particulars; elements combined form an organic whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modest terms, when compacted by harmony and rounded period, create dignity and elevation; separation dissipates power—work toward a unified, compact structure rather than disconnected fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid effeminate, hurried, or over-rhythmical movement
rubrics_metrics.description: An effeminate and hurried movement or excessive regular rhythm degrades style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of pyrrhics, trochees, and a regular dance-like cadence creates monotonous sameness; listeners may focus on tune/cadence rather than meaning, 'beating time' with the speaker. Avoid splitting sentences into many tiny words crowding cohesion ('hammered' together).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cramping diction and over-compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-compression (cutting words too short) causes deformity and fritters away force; concision should be judicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not the same as judicious compactness: do not prune words until their sense is lost. Strive for directness without destroying necessary weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-extension and unseasonable length
rubrics_metrics.description: Style becomes lifeless when relaxed into unseasonable length; excessive extension diminishes force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is required—neither undue compression nor undue extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean or petty words that degrade lofty passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean, ignoble, or vulgar expressions reduce the impressiveness of sublime descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Herodotus' 'having seethed' or 'wore away' and 'unwelcome end' are beneath the dignity of a storm description. Theopompus' mixing 'panniers and spices and bags' with gold and jewelled bowls makes a scene grotesque. Use broad strokes for grandeur; give details in one or two sweeping phrases rather than sordid particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep incongruous low details out of magnificent description
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix petty, sordid, or domestic details with majestic subjects; such inclusions stand out as deformities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either elevate the detail into a dignified large stroke ('piles of grain of every species') or omit tiny specifics; do not create the impression of describing a kitchen amid magnificence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and arrangement can ennoble common language
rubrics_metrics.description: Even writers with ordinary vocabularies can attain dignity by fine arrangement and harmony of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Philistus, Aristophanes occasionally, Euripides almost always—common words cast in a fine mould are made sublime by position and rhythmic stress. Arrangement often matters more than thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress, pacing, and delay of movement for stately effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct stress on each word and a deliberate, delayed advance can produce stately sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hurry the movement; avoid running language 'on wheels.' Arrange words so time is delayed and each word bears force, as in Euripides' lines where action is made more vivid by measured pacing.
